extracted.intended_audience: researchers, health journalists, and health communication specialists (and interested clinicians/policy-makers) interested in how news reporting affects patient/caregiver interpretation
extracted.subtask_description: Randomized-trial evaluation of how 'spin' (misrepresentation of study results) in health news stories about pharmacologic treatments affects patients' and caregivers' interpretation of treatment benefit. Trials compare news stories with spin versus versions rewritten without spin across three study types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'spin'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats 'spin' as the misrepresentation of study results in health news stories reporting studies of pharmacologic treatments; spin is the exposure variable whose effect on interpretation is being measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary outcome — participants' interpretation question and scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary outcome was participants' interpretation assessed by one specific question: "What do you think is the probability that 'treatment X' would be beneficial to patients?" (scale, 0 [very unlikely] to 10 [very likely]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a single-item numerical rating scale from 0–10 to quantify perceived probability of benefit; report means and SDs for comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention comparison — news story versions with vs without spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Two versions of the news stories were used: the version with spin and a version rewritten without spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the same news story content presented either with spin (original reported version) or in a neutral/rewritten version without spin to isolate the effect of spin on interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of studies represented in news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Each RCT considered news stories reporting a different type of study: (1) pre-clinical study, (2) phase I/II non-RCT, and (3) phase III/IV RCT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a range of underlying study types (pre-clinical through late-phase RCT) because the effect of spin may vary by study type; analyze separately by type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criterion for news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: For each type of study, we identified news stories reported with spin that had earned mention in the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select news items that were actually circulated in the press and contained spin, then prepare matched rewritten versions without spin for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial design — two-arm, parallel-group, Internet-based RCTs
rubrics_metrics.description: We conducted three two-arm, parallel-group, Internet-based randomized trials (RCTs) comparing the interpretation of news stories reported with or without spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use randomized allocation to arms (spin vs no-spin) in an online setting to measure causal effect on readers' interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant population — patients/caregivers from Inspire community
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were patients/caregivers involved in Inspire, a large online community of more than one million patients/caregivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit actual patients/caregivers (not just general public) to assess real-world interpretation; report community source and relevant demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and allocation per RCT
rubrics_metrics.description: For each RCT, 300 participants were randomly assigned to assess a news story with spin (n = 150) or without spin (n = 150), and 900 participants assessed a news story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify and report per-trial sample sizes and per-arm allocation; here 150 participants per arm provided the basis for the reported comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome reporting and statistical summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Results reported as mean (SD) scores for the primary outcome for abstracts reported with and without spin, mean differences with 95% CIs, and p-values (e.g., mean difference [95% CI] 1.7 [1.0-2.3], p < 0.001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present central tendency and dispersion (mean, SD), compute mean differences with 95% confidence intervals and p-values to quantify the effect of spin; use graphical displays (boxplots, forest plots) to illustrate distributions and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect criterion / conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were more likely to consider that the treatment would be beneficial to patients when the news story was reported with spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret a statistically and practically meaningful increase in perceived benefit (e.g., mean differences of ~1.7–2.3 on a 0–10 scale across study types) as evidence that spin affects interpretation; discuss implications for health communication and reporting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial registration and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers NCT03094078, NCT03094104, NCT03095586.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Register trials and report identifiers; provide access to protocols/registration to support transparency and reproducibility of randomized evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual and tabular summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures include flow of participants, boxplots of participants’ interpretation, and forest plots of results for primary and secondary outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide participant flow diagrams, distribution plots (median, quartiles, means), and forest plots to display effect sizes across comparisons and outcomes for clarity.
